text: The Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa will come to order. The purpose of this hearing is to examine the historical, political, and strategic context of Judea and Samaria. I now recognize myself for an opening statement. I want to begin by thanking my colleagues for being here today and our witnesses for taking the time to share their expertise with the committee. Your perspectives are invaluable as we continue examining one of the most complex issues in U.S.-Israel relations. In September, this subcommittee held a roundtable with Ambassador Huckabee to hear directly from the administration about its current efforts in Israel and its perspective on the evolving landscape in Judea and Samaria. That discussion provided valuable context on the policy challenges before us. Today's hearing builds on that foundation by taking a step back and focusing on the historical, legal, and strategic dynamics that shaped this issue. Judea and Samaria remain central to decades of diplomatic debate, negotiations, and regional tension. The region's modern history, from its role in the British Mandate to the unresolved sovereignty questions in 1948, to the Jordanian occupation from 1948 to 1967, including the displacement of Jewish communities during that period, continues to shape legal interpretations, security considerations, and international discourse today. In recent months, international discussions about the future of these territories have accelerated. To understand this, we must also understand the historical context that led us to this point. Understanding the daily realities for communities in these areas, the security challenges they face, and the implications for Israel's broader defense posture is essential to evaluating U.S. engagement and future policy discussions. Our witnesses today bring deep historical, legal, and strategic knowledge. Their testimony will help clarify key facts, illuminate longstanding debates, and provide members with the nuanced understanding needed to assess U.S. policy moving forward. Ultimately, our goal is to ensure that American policy is rooted in facts, strengthen our relationship with Israel, and support long-term stability and security across the Middle East. I now recognize the ranking member from California, Representative Sherman, for an opening statement.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should explain that I am the acting ranking member until the gentlelady from Florida deals with some issues. And those of you on the committee know that I've been here for 29 years. I've been chair and ranking member of a variety of different subcommittees, and I look forward to filling in in this role. As to this hearing, we can start with a map of Judea and Samaria, and we will see that during most of our history, the Jewish people were an inland people. Yes, indeed, Hebron was part of the Kingdom of Judea, but Tel Aviv wasn't, except when Israel or Judea reached its maximum extent, as it did at various times in its history. If we turn to any nationality and say, you define your borders based on the maximum you ever controlled in history, then Mongolia would control half of the world, the Greeks would control Anatolia, the Germans would be restored to East Prussia, and the Chumash would own my condo in the San Fernando Valley. The fact of the matter is that modern Zionism focused more on the coastal plain than the ancient Israelites or the ancient Kingdom of Judea, that the borders in 2025 should be drafted based on where people live now. Otherwise, you can call Israel a colonial settler state. Now, that ignores the Jewish tie to the land, albeit slightly different borders of ancient times, but it also ignores the fact that every group of human beings is a group of colonial settlers. That before there were Chumash in the San Fernando Valley, I'm sure there were other tribes. That before there were the Turks in Anatolia, there were the Greeks. That before there were the Poles in northern Poland, there were the Germans. And before there were the Arabs in Morocco and Egypt, these lands spoke Latin and Berber and Egyptian and Greek, and one of the greatest imperialist enterprises in the history of the world was the Arab Empire and the First and the Second Caliphates. So the question it is interesting to study history. I spend a lot of time doing it. But history should not be guiding us we shouldn't as to resolving modern problems. The slogan, From the river to the sea, is an ugly slogan, whether it is in the mouths of those who would expel or kill every Jew living west of the Jordan River, or whether it is in the hands of those who would permanently disenfranchise, and in a few cases or a few extremist politicians, expel the Arabs living in that same area. Now, the Palestinians have never lost an opportunity to lose their state. If we can put up the second chart. In 1947, the Jews of Israel accepted this 1947 map. As you can see, the majority of the populated areas are in the hands of the Arabs who now call themselves Arab Palestinians. So then we see the 1966 borders. We also don't have a map of it, but we see the Palestinian state that was offered by President Clinton with the approval of Israel in his last weeks in office. Again and again, to the amazement of the world, Palestinian leaders representing less military power demand total control of all the land. It is hard to recognize how unreasonable their bargaining position is because we're used to the ones the side that has the less military power accepting the more reasonable bargaining position. So I look forward to learning some history here, Mr. Chairman, but I am not going to focus my beliefs on how we should design peace in the Middle East on a discussion of whether the Samaritans were Jews or whether they're a separate group. And I yield back.

We are pleased to have a distinguished panel of witnesses before us today on this important topic: Professor Eugene Kontorovich, the senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation; Mr. Morton Klein, the president of the Zionist Organization of America; and Dr. Jon Alterman, the Brzezinski Chair in Global Security and Geostrategy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Chairman Lawler, Ranking Member Sherman, and honorable members of the committee, thank you for inviting me to speak on the topic of Judea and Samaria at this hearing. Let's start by discussing what is Judea and Samaria. It's a geographic name for the hilly regions north and south of Jerusalem. It's largely synonymous with the term West Bank, which the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan gave to the area when it conquered it and annexed it in 1950. Regardless of the name, some claim that this territory is currently under belligerent occupation by the State of Israel and that international law places numerous restrictions on Israel's presence and conduct there. I will explain how, according to the rules of international law applied everywhere else in the world, the territory is not occupied, and in fact Israel has a strong sovereign claim to it. In May 1948, the Mandate for Palestine came to an end, and the State of Israel was established. Five Arab armies immediately invaded, seeking to prevent the establishment of the Jewish state. President Truman, however, promptly recognized, quote, "the Jewish state" proclaimed in Palestine. So what were Israel's borders when it was created in May 1948? In international law, there is a simple, clear rule to determine the borders of new countries. Under the doctrine of uti possidetis juris, a new country automatically inherits the borders of the last top-level administrative unit in the area. In other words, pre-independence internal boundaries carry over to become the external boundaries of the new state. The continuity of prior borders is the sole deciding factor, trumping fuzzy and hard-to-administer considerations like self-determination, and as the ranking member pointed out, historical title and historical presence. The rule is a matter of textbook international law, and the reasons for it are clear. Demographics and history give rise to multiple competing claims, whereas uti possidetis provides a unique, unambiguous solution. Take, for example, Crimea. The territory had been part of Russia and the Russian Empire for most of the past several hundred years. The majority of the inhabitants were Russian speakers. Yet the international community rightly considers Russia's annexation of the territory illegal and regards it as Ukrainian territory to this day. The reason is simple. It is the uti possidetis juris principle. Nikita Khrushchev had redrawn the internal borders of the Soviet Union to place Ukraine in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. It had previously been in the Russian Soviet Socialist Republic, a fairly arbitrary decision on his part. When the Soviet Union collapsed and Ukraine became a state, it automatically inherited the borders of the last top-level unit, the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. So when Israel gained independence, the preceding geopolitical entity was Mandatory Palestine, which included Judea and Samaria. That's not in dispute. So Israel's borders upon independence automatically extended to all of the mandatory territory it succeeded to. Indeed, throughout the Middle East—Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Jordan—the states that had been League of Nations mandates to this day still have the borders of the mandatory territory. In each of these countries, the mandatory borders were drawn in ways that included discontented minorities unhappy to be part of the larger state, be it Muslims in then-Christian Lebanon or Kurds in Iraq. But in none of these cases have such arguments been seen as a reason to redraw the new borders. Now, Jordan and its allies failed at wiping out the Jewish state in 1948, but they did occupy much of Palestine, including Judea and Samaria. It ethnically cleansed every single Jew from this area. When Israel took these areas in 1967, it was not occupying foreign territory, but rather taking territory to which it had sovereign title since 1948, sovereign rights. Imagine if Ukraine dislodged Russia from Crimea. Would anyone say that Ukraine was now occupying Crimea because Russia had administered it for so long? The neutral application of these rules can very be clearly can be clearly seen in the Karabakh conflict. A majority-Armenian region within Azerbaijan with a deep Armenian history. Armenia took control of it in a war with Azerbaijan at the time of the country's independence in the early '90s. Yet since Baku captured the territory in 2023, no one treats it as an occupying power. The reason is simple. Karabakh had been within the boundaries of the Azeri Soviet Socialist Republic and automatically becomes part of the state of Azerbaijan. So under widely agreed international rules, Israel has sovereign rights to the territory. The legal principles are not controversial. Some just want to create a unique carve-out for the Jewish state. To conclude, let me turn to practical applications. Some who believe the road for peace depend on the creation of a sovereign Palestinian state may worry that the legal analysis here prevents that. That is not the case. The law is neutral to diplomatic solutions. Israel's sovereign rights to the territory does not prevent and indeed enables it to cede some or all of it for the creation of a separate Palestinian state. What the legal analysis does make clear is there is nothing about the 1949 armistice lines that make them the legally mandated or even presumptive borders of such a state. I thank you for your time and attention.
Thank you, Professor Kontorovich. Thank you, Professor Kontorovich. I now recognize Mr. Klein for an opening statement.

Thank you, Chairman Lawler, Ranking Member Sherman, members of the committee. I'm president of the country's oldest pro-Israel organization, the Zionist Organization of America, ZOA. We're dedicated to advancing mutually beneficial U.S.-Israel alliance, combating antisemitism, and ensuring the safety of both America and Israel. Before that, I was in medical research, working for many years with the two-time Nobel Prize winner Linus Pauling at Stanford University. The Jewish people are called Jews because we are from Judea. We are Judeans. Jew is a contraction of the word Judean. We are Judea and Samaria's indigenous people. American leaders have long recognized this. President John Adams wrote, I really wish the Jews would reestablish Judea as an independent Jewish nation. Other presidents, from Lincoln to Truman, have urged Judea and Samaria, then the region of Palestine, to become a Jewish state. Judea and Samaria is the historic Jewish homeland where Jews lived for thousands of years. This is where the first Jew, Abraham, purchased his and Sarah's burial place, where God first speaks to Abraham promising Judea and Samaria to him, which was the beginning of the Jewish connection to Judea and Samaria; where the Jews Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, Ruth, Leah are buried in the Cave of Machpelah, one of the holiest Jewish places in Judaism. Here was the first capital under King David. The Jew Jacob slept and dreamt here. The Jew Joseph is buried there. The Jewish tabernacle, the Ark of the Covenant, stood there for 369 years. And the Maccabees, the heroes of the Hanukkah story, lived and established their base to reclaim Israel and the Jewish temple and built fortresses there to protect the Jewish people. Exodus in the Bible relates that Moses and Joshua led the Jewish people to their homeland in Judea and Samaria. Jews have had a continuous presence there for over 3,000 years. The Jewish spiritual and historical connection has never severed or lapsed for Jews. Judea and Samaria was in the heart of the Jewish kingdoms that existed for hundreds of years. King David and Solomon unified Jewish kingdoms. Jews lived in Hebron, the oldest Jewish community in the world, until the infamous massacre of Hebron's innocent Jews in 1929, but came back in 1935. By contrast, Arabs hail from Arabia and North Africa. They are not indigenous to Judea and Samaria. There was never a Palestinian Arab state in Judea and Samaria, even when they controlled it from '48 to '67. Palestine is a Roman name, not an Arab name. The Romans renamed Judea and Samaria and surrounding areas Palestine after the Jewish enemy, the Philistines, to cause pain to the Jews and to try to de-Judaize the area. Arabs can't even pronounce the letter P. They can't say Palestine; they say Falastin. Judea and Samaria, moreover, is legally Jewish land. A series of binding international agreements—the San Remo Resolution, League of Nations Covenant, British Mandate, Lodge-Fish, UN Charter Article 80—recognized the Jewish people's connection to the land and guaranteed the land of Israel under international law, including Judea and Samaria, to the Jewish people. UN resolutions that contradict the UN Charter are absolutely legally void. In '48 and '49, Jordan attacked and illegally seized Judea and Samaria. Jordan killed or expelled the Jews, illegally occupied the area for 19 years, only recognized by two countries, and renamed Judea and Samaria the West Bank in order to de-Judaize it. In fact, the initial PLO Charter, Article 24, explicitly states that the PLO has no territorial claims over Judea and Samaria and Gaza. And Jordan relinquished their claims in 1988. The PLO sought Israel's destruction then as now, as the Palestinian demand is likewise not about a state. It's about destroying Israel and murdering Jews and Christians. This is the emblem of the Palestinian Authority showing all of Israel with a keffiyeh over all of it, a picture of Arafat, and the rifle, a Kalashnikov rifle. This is not the emblem you use if you want peace with the Jewish State of Israel. This is a picture of one of the suicide bombers. They do pictures and posters of every suicide bomber, and honoring him as a hero and a martyr, and put this up in universities and high schools throughout Judea and Samaria. This is not what you do if you want peace with the Jewish state. The Arabs were offered a state, rejected it eight times since the Peel Commission in '37, three times in the last 20 years. In '67, Jordan attacked Israel again. In that war, Israel regained the lawful lands of Judea and Samaria. Today, there are 500,000 Jews living in Judea and Samaria. This is Jewish land legally, religiously, biblically, politically, and morally. Judea and Samaria are strategically located for Israel's security. If they give it up, Judea and Samaria, it'll only be 8 miles wide. The Oslo Accords have made clear that a Palestinian state would result in disaster. When they withdrew, when Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005, 9,000 Jews left, 30,000 rockets, and October 7th happened. When under the Oslo Accords, when Jews gave up land, terrorism reigned supreme, with 10,000 innocent Jews being killed. The Palestinian Authority pays $400 million a year for lifetime pensions for terrorists to murder Jews. Arab terrorists in Jenin and Samaria are launching rockets at Israel right now. Only this week they found manufacturing rockets that are going on there. Establishing a Palestinian state would send a terrible message that terrorism pays. There are 21 Arab states and one little Jewish state. That's the yellow. It's 600 times the size of the Arab world. We need peace. If Israel doesn't have control of the Jewish heartland in Judea and Samaria, peace will be impossible. Again, Judea and Samaria, Jewish Israeli land, is Jewish land legally, religiously, biblically, politically, morally. This is what's best for America. This is what's best for Israel. Thank you very, very much.
Thank you, Mr. Klein. I now recognize Dr. Alterman for an opening statement.

Chairman Lawler, Ranking Member Sherman, distinguished members, thank you for the opportunity to talk with you today. The West Bank presents us with one of the hardest policy challenges we face. It's difficult because it combines ancient history, modern security threats, and deeply held religious beliefs. And here's what makes this especially complex. Even Israel's strongest supporters disagree about fundamental questions. President Trump has been clear. He told Time magazine that Israel would lose all support if it annexed the West Bank. Vice President Vance said the same thing after visiting Israel. Yet some of Israel's closest friends in Congress and the evangelical community see this matter very differently. If we're honest with ourselves, we need to recognize that not only are there competing claims here, but there are competing legitimate claims. And that's if we just consider what's clear from the historical record. When we bring in faith, values, and interests which aren't universal, the issue becomes even more complicated. I'm not here to advocate for one side or another or tell you who's right. I'm here to suggest that we're not dealing with a problem with one clear answer. Let me share a story. In my youth, I worked for Senator Moynihan during the Northern Ireland conflict. For decades, people said that conflict was unsolvable: ancient hatreds, religious divisions, antagonists at each other's throats. And a lot of Irish Americans were sending money to the IRA, which was killing civilians, and Moynihan and three other Irish American politicians came together to dial down the temperature. A decade later, former Senator George Mitchell helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement, it was a 34-page agreement that left much unsaid. It spawned hundreds and hundreds of pages of clarifications, elaborations, and amendments. It didn't end disagreements, but it certainly did end the fighting, and Northern Ireland is a different place and a better place. That should be our principal goal, not finding a solution to this conflict today, but creating conditions where solutions become possible and then become real. Right now, we're headed in the wrong direction. When Hamas attacked Israel on October 7th, it wanted to isolate Israel in the world, end Israel's normalization with Arab countries, and make everyone lose hope. We cannot let them win. Israel worked hard for international acceptance since its founding. The Abraham Accords showed how previously unimaginable things are possible. But while some Israelis covet the lands of historic Judea and Samaria, 3 million Muslim and Christian Arabs live there. About 20% of Israeli citizens are already non-Jewish Arabs. Israel can't extend citizenship to Palestinians in the West Bank without fundamentally changing its character. Palestinians can't continue indefinitely with no clear legal status, and Israel's efforts to constrain Arabs' daily lives builds resentment, not acceptance. Ethnic cleansing would make Israel a complete pariah. Arab governments won't accept the current situation indefinitely, and neither will much of the world. Nobody has a perfect solution, not me, not anybody else. But I know that these solutions can't be imposed from the outside, and unilateral actions won't advance Israel's security. So what should America do? First, resist steps that foreclose future options. When we close doors, we make peace harder, not easier. Second, preserve space for negotiation. The parties themselves must find the way forward, but we can help keep that pathway open. Third, focus on improving daily life. Israelis and Palestinians alike who still hope for dignity, security, and peace deserve our support. Mr. Chairman, we can't solve this problem for them, but we can help ensure that resolution remains possible. After decades of violence and disappointment, that may not sound like much, but right now it might be everything. Thank you.

Thank you, Dr. Alterman. I now recognize myself for 5 minutes of questions. This hearing serves an important purpose to educate everyone here and everyone watching at home about Judea and Samaria, or, as commonly known as, the West Bank. We speak so freely about this territory in Congress and in conversations across the country. And I think it's really important that we're actually all on the same page about what exactly we're talking about, especially when we talk about the potential for a Palestinian state in the future. So this map behind me is a current map of Judea and Samaria. The map is color-coded to showcase the different areas located within what is referred to as the West Bank. Area A, in burgundy, is the only area with full control by the Palestinian Authority. Area B, which is more of a mustard color, is under PA administrative control, but Israel has certain security responsibilities there. And then Area C, which is the rest of the map, the beige color, and covers over 60% of the land, is under Israeli civilian and security control. So when people say the West Bank, this is what we're actually talking about. So, Mr. Klein, why do you think fully understanding the makeup of Judea and Samaria is helpful for members of Congress as we talk about long-term resolutions to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict and other topics at present time?

Oh, sorry. Thank you. Israel has allowed— has given away all of Gaza, given administrative control to 40% of Judea and Samaria. This is where 99% of the Palestinian Arabs live. They live under their own rule. Nobody is occupying them. They have their own parliament, their own TV and radio, their own media, their own police force, their own businesses. It's important for people to understand this. And it's important for people to understand that Israel has offered a state to the Palestinians eight times in the last 80 years, starting with the Peel Commission in 1937, last with Ehud Olmert in 2008. Olmert offered them 97% of Judea and Samaria, 3% of Israel, and half of Jerusalem. They said no. I asked Ehud Olmert personally, Mr. Prime Minister, how could Abbas have turned you down? There was no compromise, you gave them everything. And he said, Abbas said he won't sign an agreement that says we support Israel as a Jewish state. 'I won't sign it.' We want— we will not— to have a limit to the number of Arabs that can move into Israel to 150,000, 'I won't sign it.' To have a clause that says there'll be no further claims, 'We will have further claims whenever we want.' So it's important to understand the history of this region and what was offered in Judea and Samaria that was turned down eight times in the last 80 years.
